title: Remotely unplugging a USB device on my Mac, without touching it
content:
Tonight I was remote debugging a USB-C device with custom firmware, which was plugged into my Mac Studio at work. I was accessing it over a WireGuard VPN tunnel.

Part of the debugging process involves flashing firmware to the device using MIDI SysEx messages, and while handy, this technique can also be flaky, leaving the device in a partially-flashed state that needs a physical re-plug to recover from.

title: Who gets to decide if something is written by AI?
content:
Every day there’s some new argument about whether something was written by AI: a writing prize where the winning story was supposedly AI-generated, or an author who lost her contract after the manuscript lit up Pangram1, or a dispute about whether a tweet was written by a human or not.

Why do people hate Pangram so much?

You could have an interesting conversation about whether Pangram is reliable2, or whether it’s wrong to run AI detection tools on other people’s writing3. However, I think these points are downstream of the real source of conflict, which is that many anti-AI people have a fundamental hatred of AI detection tooling.

This puzzled me for a long time. If you hate AI, shouldn’t you love a tool that can unmask it? If you’re worried about the intrusion of AI-generated content into human spaces, shouldn’t you be thrilled that there are systems that can identify and flag content like this? Shouldn’t people who think AI is wrong be advocating for mandatory Pangram scanning of all social media, news, education, and so on — or if they don’t trust the Pangram company specifically, shouldn’t they be advocating for the government to build a Pangram-for-the-public tool4 to capture these social goods? Why5 aren’t they doing any of this?

I think it’s about power. In particular, I think that the question “who gets to decide if something is written by AI” is a question about who should wield power: the power to gatekeep literary prizes, to fail or pass students, to exclude people from the public discourse, and so on. That probably sounds bad, but if my blog has a central thesis it would be that “everything is actually about power and that’s fine”, so I’m actually fairly sympathetic to Pangram skeptics.

Tool-shaped solutions

Let me try and present their view in the best possible light. Suppose you’re worried about AI intrusion into public spaces because you think this gives the tech sector an unprecedented amount of social power, not (like me) because you just find it unpleasant to read AI slop. On this view, it is entirely rational to dislike tools like Pangram being made the arbiter of whether something is AI writing, because Pangram is culturally and politically part of the same tech sector that you distrust in the first place. If you don’t want Sam Altman or Dario Amodei with a hand on the wheel of public opinion, having some other tech CEO as a watchdog is unlikely to reassure you much.

In fact, distrust of tool-shaped solutions in general is also entirely rational. The history of the last few decades has been a shift towards legible tool-based processes and away from messy community-based ones. You now book a taxi ride (or a hotel, or a doctor’s appointment) entirely in an app instead of having to talk to a human. Software has made many low-level jobs semi-robotic: the system tells you what to do and assesses your performance, instead of a human who can make allowances. Many anti-AI people are anti-AI because they think6 this shift in general has been a disaster for humanity, and that we must return to less efficient, more human-centered systems. To these people, the idea of ameliorating AI by relying on yet another AI tool probably sounds like some kind of sick joke.

Community self-policing

So why am I pro-Pangram? Because, as far as I can see, the only alternative7 to AI detection tooling is relying on communities to self-police. If the literary prize committee investigates8 and determines there was no AI use, then that’s that. If the community agrees that something was written by AI, then it was. Here’s where I part ways with the AI haters, because I think this is terrible.

People who do not use AI are not good at judging whether some text was AI-generated. I see this a lot on Twitter, where a piece of text that has obvious AI tells is being judged by people who just haven’t read enough AI content to recognize them, or a tweet that has obvious human tells is being judged as AI purely because it’s long and polite. If you delegate this kind of judgment to AI haters, they will get it wrong more often than not.

If you care about keeping AI away from human arenas of art and culture, you should be willing to use the most powerful tools available, even if they are technically also AI tools9. If you have a (sensible) distrust of tech companies to police each other, you should be pushing for open-source solutions or lobbying governments to build their own AI-detection platforms in-house. A world where “was this written by AI” is left up to the community is a world with more AI-written stories, articles and poetry in it.

  1. Currently the best AI-detection tool.

    ↩

  2. My view is “yes, obviously”. The contrary view is something like this, which I find woefully unconvicing: Pangram (and its third-party tests) do report false positives and negatives on the same dataset, and has clearly gone to great lengths to train on a huge variety of content.

    ↩

  3. My view is “no, obviously”: Pangram does not train on user data and any published works have already been scraped.

    ↩

  4. Incidentally, I think this is a really good idea and could be done far more cheaply than most “government getting into AI” schemes I see.

    ↩

  5. I confess here I’m falling into the trap of diagnosis, but I do think the core argument (that tools like Pangram work) is solid and unrelated.

    ↩

  6. I don’t know what to think about this on a factual level, but on a vibes level I am very uncomfortable with these arguments.

    ↩

  7. People lie, drafts can be generated after the fact, there is no plausible cryptographic path to attestation, C2PA is not the right tool for the job, and so on.

    ↩

  8. I assume it goes without saying that ordinary investigation is useless here: skilled AI writing will often have drafts, contemporaneous conversations with peers, and all the other hallmarks of “real” writing.

    ↩

  9. I think the distinction is entirely vacuous, but in case you don’t: Pangram is definitely not generative AI.

    ↩

title: How did pinwheel calculators work?
content:
As a handful of readers might know, I am a bit of a calculator nerd. I’m especially fond of mechanical four-function calculators that had their heyday between the 1920s and 1960s and then disappeared without a trace.

A video is worth a thousand tokens, so to explore the ingenuity of these designs, let’s start with a short clip of a Vaucanson calculator from my collection:

In the first half of the video, I demonstrate addition. I calculate 1234 + 4321 by placing the first operand in the input register (top), turning the crank clockwise to add this value to the accumulator (bottom right), and then entering the second operand and cranking again. To subtract from the stored value, I’d instead turn the crank counterclockwise.

The second and more interesting half shows multiplication: I solve 79 × 123 by entering the first operand and then turning the crank three times to load 79 × 3 into the accumulator. Next, I shift the accumulator carriage one decimal digit to the right and crank twice; because the accumulator is offset from the input register, this has the same effect as cranking twenty times in the original position; in other words, I add 79 × 20. Finally, I shift the carriage once more and complete one more turn to add 79 × 100. Note that the crank counter in the bottom left now reads “123”, confirming that we multiplied the first operand by the correct value.

To divide, I’d load the first operand into the accumulator and then successively subtract power-of-ten multiples of the second number. This would give me the integer result in the counter register and the remainder in the accumulator.

Alright — so how does this work? Well, if you pop open a pinwheel calculator, you will be greeted by a pretty complicated mechanism:

There’s a lot going on here, but the most important part of the assembly is the cylindrical stack of input disks, one per digit, as seen in the top right of the photo. Each disk has three main components: a center section mounted to a keyed shaft that stays in position until the main crank is turned; a set of nine radial pins that slide into grooves in that disk; and a freely-moving digit-setting ring with a track and a couple of detent positions:

Each pin has a protrusion that rides in the track of the digit-setting ring. By turning the input lever one way or the other, we can change the number of pins that extend from the assembly.

When the crank is turned, the entire assembly rotates and these extended pins mesh to an intermediate gear that advances the digit at the corresponding position of the accumulator:

Of course, this mechanism is not enough: without a way to carry to the next column, 0001 + 0009 would give us 0000 instead of 0010. To implement carry, each input disk (except for the rightmost one) is also equipped with a spring-loaded carry pin. This pin sticks out at all times, but is normally out of the path of the intermediate gear — offset to the right — so it has no effect on the output value.

To actually perform carry, each digit of the accumulator is equipped with a cam that shoves a wedge-shaped carry-sensing lever into the path of the carry pin just as the value rolls over from 9 to 0. This wedge in turn deflects the carry pin to the left, momentarily placing it in the path of the intermediate gear for the next decimal digit.

This is a mouthful; the entire process is shown in the following video:

The carry-sensing lever is pushed back into the home position before the drum completes a full rotation, thus resetting the mechanism.

Note that the carry pins are staggered and do not engage at all once; this is to allow carry to effortlessly ripple through all digits if necessary (e.g., when adding 9999 + 1).

There’s a couple of additional convenience and reliability features in each pinwheel calculator; this includes interlocks to prevent out-of-sequence inputs, as well as reset levers for each register. There’s even a mechanical bell on overflow or underflow. I won’t bore you with all the gory details, in part because these mechanisms are less interesting — but if you’re morbidly curious, this ancient YouTube video provides a more complete walkthrough.

And if you want to learn about the prehistory of calculators, I invite you to check out my 2023 article:

PS. Yep, this is why one of the registers on all Intel CPUs, used as the implicit destination for some opcodes, is called the “accumulator”.

title: What happens when you put a non-agile object in the CoreApplication Properties?
content:
Last time, we noticed that non-agile objects in the Core­Application.Properties appear to behave differently from agile objects.

I mean, it looks like they behave differently, but that’s only because you are taking too narrow a view.

They behave the same if you interpret the rule as “The objects remain alive until there are no more apartments that can access them.” Non-agile objects can be used only from the apartment that created them, whereas agile objects can be used from any apartment. Therefore, non-agile objects expire when their host apartment shuts down, whereas agile objects expire when all apartments shut down.

The Core­Application.Properties uses Ro­Get­Agile­Reference to wrap the non-agile object so that it can safely be stored. (Really, it just uses Ro­Get­Agile­Reference to wrap all objects, but an agile wrapper around an agile object is a nop.)

Internally, Ro­Get­Agile­Reference has a variety of mechanisms for creating the agile reference, depending on the flags you pass, but they all have the property that the reference to a non-agile object is released when the apartment shuts down. The observed behavior is coming from Ro­Get­Agile­Reference, not from Core­Application.Properties.

Now, the Properties collection doesn’t know that the agile reference refers to an expired object. It’s just holding onto the agile reference, waiting to return it when requested.

So let’s try to access the expired object and see what happens.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <winrt/Windows.ApplicationModel.Core.h>
#include <winrt/Windows.Foundation.Collections.h>

struct NonAgile : winrt::implements<NonAgile,                  
    winrt::Windows::Foundation::IInspectable, winrt::non_agile>
{                                                              
    ~NonAgile() { printf("Expired!\n"); }                      
};                                                             

int main()
{
    winrt::init_apartment(winrt::apartment_type::single_threaded);

    std::thread t([] {
        winrt::init_apartment(winrt::apartment_type::single_threaded);
        winrt::Windows::ApplicationModel::Core::CoreApplication::Properties().
            Insert(L"meow", winrt::make<NonAgile>());
        winrt::uninit_apartment();
        });

    t.join();

    bool present =                                                        
    winrt::Windows::ApplicationModel::Core::CoreApplication::Properties().
        HasKey(L"meow");                                                  
    printf("Has the value: %s\n", present ? "true" : "false");            

    auto value =                                                              
        winrt::Windows::ApplicationModel::Core::CoreApplication::Properties().
        Lookup(L"meow");                                                      
    printf("Has a value? %s\n", value ? "true" : "false");                    

    winrt::uninit_apartment();
    return 0;
}

I added a message when the non-agile object is destructed so you can see (by stepping through the code) that it happens when the secondary thread calls uninit_apartment to shut down its single-threaded apartment. This is the Global Interface Table relinquishing its reference at apartment shutdown.

After we put the non-agile object in the Properties and then shut down its apartment, the non-agile object is destroyed, but the entry remains in the Properties, which we can confirm by seeing that HasKey() still returns true. The key-value pair is still present in the Properties.

However, if we try to retrieve the value, the Lookup fails with an exception because the entry is now poisoned: It is a reference to an already-destroyed object.¹ You can’t retrieve the poisoned entry; all you can do is remove it.

Next time, we’ll look at how all this fits into the original problem of creating a fake agile wrapper that is technically agile but is not useful outside its home apartment because the original object refuses to be marshaled.

¹ The specific error that is returned is E_INVALID­ARG because the Global interface Table entry is no longer valid. This specific error code is a leaky abstraction. If the developers had thought about it, they could have added code to transform the error into something more appropriate like RPC_E_SERVER_DIED.

The post What happens when you put a non-agile object in the CoreApplication Properties? appeared first on The Old New Thing.

title: BREAKING: Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are panicking
content:
For several years I have worried about the fact that, as I once put it, LLMs are like “bull[s] in a china shop, reckless and hard to control.”

Unfortunately, the situation hasn’t gotten any better. The link above happens to be about something that I wrote in 2022, on Christmas Day, anticipating the release of GPT-4, but the key point is this: it has been true of every model since. Hundreds of them.

And important, breaking reporting discussed below suggests that the situation is apparently about to get much worse.

It is not an exaggeration to say that the industry is now facing a crisis that could affect all of us. Generative AI has gotten harder to monitor, harder to control, and more reckless, to the point where it sounds like many people working in the industry are genuinely scared.

Technical advances on so-called “capabilities” have NOT been accompanied by technical advances in being able to interpret and control models.

Turning them into agents with internet access has made them fundamentally more dangerous. The issue isn’t whether the models are “powerful” (a rather vague word) but whether the models can be controlled, and whether they are empowered to roam the internet.

Unfortunately, it appears that although they have been empowered to roam the internet, they cannot be controlled, and we cannot trust them to act in what Stuart Russell calls “human compatible” ways. As we have seen repeatedly over the last six months, we can’t. Whether you think the models are “smart” (whatever that means) it is clear that they don’t have enough common sense to refrain from harm.

Worse, we still have not set up the kind of independent of scientific panels for FDA-like review that I have long advocated for—which has left society almost entirely unprepared for what’s about to come.

And even worse than that, dysfunction in Washington—and an insistence on neutered measures like self-policing—has left decisions about what gets released to CEOs with enormous financial conflicts of interest.

The breaking news is this: dozens of employees, as Madison Mills reports at Axios, are now freaking out, quite possibly with good reason. (Click the link above for the full story, and/or click the tweet below for a summary.)

From what I gather, those debates are at the highest levels of the company. As ever some of this may be PR, but some of it seems to reflect genuine fear.

§

Because so much of the immediate problem stems from the large-scale deployment of agents with internet access, there is a simple short-term fix: the AI companies should voluntarily pull agents with internet access off the market until they have adequate safety solutions.

And they should not release new models if they don’t have consensus internally about whether those models are safe.

Ever.

If they won’t do the right things voluntarily, the federal government should step in.
